newsitem.title: USA: ATHLETICS-AGUTA, ROBA WIN 101ST BOSTON MARATHON.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-AGUTA, ROBA WIN 101ST BOSTON MARATHON.

text.p: Lameck Aguta broke away from a pack of five runners late in the race and cruised to a comfortable victory in the 101st Boston Marathon on Monday, becoming the fifth Kenyan to win in seven years.

Ethiopia's Fatuma Roba, surprise gold medalist in the Atlanta Olympic marathon, proved she is a legitimate force by pulling away from South Africa's Elana Meyer for a dominating victory in the women's division.
The 25-year-old Aguta, who had two fourth-place finishes in three previous Boston attempts, posted a winning time of two hours 10 minutes and 34 seconds in the world's oldest annual marathon.
"It was magic," said Aguta, who raced away from two of his compatriots and a pair of world-class Mexican marathoners about 24.5-miles (39.4 km) into the race for his victory.
"I have been training for this all my life," added Aguta, who had trained in Kenya with defending champion Moses Tanui, who finished fifth.

Fellow Kenyan Joseph Kamau finished second in 2:10:46, followed by three-time London Marathon winner Dionicio Ceron of Mexico at 2:10:59 and two-time New York Marathon winner German Silva of Mexico, who was fourth in 2:11:21.
Tanui, who said he suffered from bronchitis over the last week, rounded out the top five in 2:11:38.
More than 10,400 runners took part in the race, run through eight communities before ending in downtown Boston.
Cosmas Ndeti of Kenya, whose three-year reign as Boston champion was ended by Tanui last year, finished a disappointing 27th. Ndeti said after the race that he suffered from malaria in February.
Roba's victory ended a three-year stranglehold on the women's title by Uta Pippig of Germany.

Pippig, the darling of the Boston fans who suffered leg injuries at the Olympics which curtailed her training for some five months, could not keep up with Roba and her South African pursuers and finished fourth.
Roba, 26, took the outright lead at the top of "Heartbreak Hill" at the 22-mile (35.4 km) mark and was never again challenged. She posted a winning time of 2:26:23.
Meyer, who broke Pippig's half-marathon world record earlier this year, finished second in 2:27:09, with fellow South African Colleen De Reuck third in 2:28:03. Pippig clocked 2:28:51.
Roba, largely unknown before the Atlanta Games, shrugged off the notorious climb known as Heartbreak Hill which had been the demise of so many runners over the past century.
"I am told there is a hill in the race, but I did not find it difficult," she said through an interpreter.
She looked comfortable the entire race, and De Reuck said she thought Roba looked strong and was toying with the field before she pulled away.
"I'm quite tired but it looks like I'm not tired," Roba said after the race. "Even though I had doubts from the beginning, when I arrived at the end I knew I could win," she added.
Mexicans Ceron and Silva were making their Boston debuts and presented a serious challenge to the Kenyans, who had claimed seven of the top eight places last year.

For much of the time Ceron led the tightly-bunched group of five runners once they left the rest of the field in the dust. Silva was the first of the five leaders to fall away and Ceron finally could not keep pace with the Kenyans.
"This has been one of the most strong and most competitive races I've ever run in," Ceron said.
Second-place finisher Kamau said the Mexicans posed a tough challenge, but the course favoured the Kenyans.

"If it was a smooth race, the Mexicans would have won the race. If it was rough, it was going to be our time," he said. "That's why I decided to make the race as hard as possible," said Kamau, who held the lead much of the race.

A strong field and near-perfect weather conditions of sunny skies, temperatures in the mid-50s (12 C) and a slight easterly breeze were expected to contribute to a fast pace. But the field got off to a surprisingly conservative start and the final times were well off the quick finishes of the recent London and Rotterdam marathons.
